context: At each new heaven Dante looks first at Beatrice, and her beauty has grown with every step up. This time something is different.

note: Until now Beatrice's smile has greeted each new heaven, brighter every time. In the seventh it would be more than a living man could bear, so she holds it back. She smiles again in Canto 23, once Dante's sight has been strengthened.

context: Beatrice's smile would do to Dante what Jupiter's unveiled glory did to Semele.

quote: the stairs of the eternal palace
note: The heavens, one above another, which Dante and Beatrice have been climbing like the steps of a palace.

context: Dante and Beatrice have risen from Jupiter, the heaven of just rulers, to the heaven of the contemplatives.

note: The constellation Leo. In the spring of 1300 the planet Saturn stood in Leo. Astrologers thought Saturn cold and Leo hot, so the planet's influence reaches the earth mixed with the Lion's.
The planet Saturn, which reflects God's light as a mirror does. Dante is to make his eyes mirrors in turn, so that they catch what is about to appear in it.

quote: weighing one joy against the other
note: The joy of looking at Beatrice against the joy of obeying her. Only someone who knew how hard it was to look away could measure how glad he was to do as she asked.
The god Saturn, who in Roman myth ruled the world during the Golden Age, a time of peace and innocence with no crime and no war. The planet carries his name.

context: The ladder rises from Saturn out of sight, toward the highest heaven. It stands for contemplation, the climb of the mind toward God. Canto 22 names it as the ladder Jacob saw.

note: Gold fits the planet of the Golden Age. It is also the most precious metal, as contemplation was held to be the highest form of life.
The souls of the contemplatives: monks and hermits who gave their lives to prayer and to thinking on God. Like all the blessed since the heaven of Mercury, they appear only as lights.
Dante's birds are jackdaws, small crows that flock at dawn. The simile describes the souls' movements on the ladder: some climb back up, some go down and return, some circle where they are.

quote: she from whom I await the how and when
note: Beatrice. Dante has learned to wait for her sign before he speaks to a soul.

quote: in the sight of Him who sees everything
note: The blessed look on God, and in God they see all things, including Dante's unspoken thoughts. This is why Beatrice and the souls so often answer questions he has not asked aloud.
In every heaven so far the souls have sung. Saturn is silent, which suits the contemplatives, whose life on earth was one of silence.

quote: for the same reason that Beatrice has not smiled
note: The song of this heaven would overwhelm Dante's mortal hearing, as her smile would overwhelm his sight. The silence is a mercy to him, not a lack of joy.

quote: Greater love did not make me more ready
note: The soul did not come because he loves Dante more than the others do. Souls higher on the ladder love as much or more, as their brightness shows. He came because God gave him the task, and the blessed do God's will gladly.

Dante asks why God chose this soul and not another: a question about predestination, God's eternal choosing of each creature's part. The eagle in Canto 20 has just warned mortals against judging such things.
The souls of Paradise show joy by shining and by spinning. This one is glad to answer, even though the answer will be that there is no answer.

quote: A divine light is directed upon me
note: How the blessed see God. No created mind can see God by its own power, so God sends a light that strengthens the soul's sight. Theologians called it the light of glory.

quote: I match the brightness of my fire
note: A rule that holds throughout Paradise: a soul shines as brightly as it sees God clearly. Vision comes first, then love and joy, and the light is the sign of them.

context: Not even the angel who sees God most clearly could say why God chooses as he does.

note: The reasons for God's choices lie in God's own will, deeper than any created mind can see. The blessed see God, but they do not see all that is in him.
A message Dante is to carry back to the living: stop trying to work out the secret of predestination. The warning is aimed at the theologians of his day as much as at ordinary believers.

quote: The mind that shines here smolders on earth
note: Dante's Italian says the mind gives off smoke on earth. A mind that is clear light in Heaven is clouded in the body. If it cannot answer this question even in Heaven, it has no chance below.
The Apennines, the mountain chain that runs down the middle of Italy between the Adriatic Sea on the east and the Tyrrhenian Sea on the west.
Monte Catria, a peak of the Apennines near Gubbio, on the border of Umbria and the Marche.
The monastery of Fonte Avellana, on the slopes of Monte Catria. Its monks lived as hermits under a strict rule of fasting, silence and prayer. It still stands.
Food dressed with nothing but olive oil: the plain fare of a fast, with no meat or animal fat.

The word that defines this heaven. Medieval Christians set two ways of life side by side: the active life of work and service, and the contemplative life of prayer and thought fixed on God. They ranked the contemplative life higher, as a foretaste of Heaven.

quote: That cloister used to yield abundantly
note: The monastery once sent a rich harvest of souls to Heaven. Now, he says, it yields nothing, and its decline will soon be exposed. Most of the saints in these upper heavens end with a complaint of this kind about their own orders.

context: He names himself only after describing the mountain and the hermitage where he lived as a monk.

note: A disputed line. Peter Damian signed his letters "Peter the sinner", and on this reading he used that name at a monastery of Saint Mary near Ravenna. But the Italian can also mean "Peter the Sinner was in the house": a different man, Pietro degli Onesti, who founded such a house near Ravenna and was often confused with Damian.

The cardinal's hat. Peter Damian was made a cardinal in 1057, against his will. The red hat itself was first given to cardinals in the thirteenth century, long after his death, so Dante is using the sign of the office in his own day.
Each holder of the office is worse than the last. A saint who was himself a cardinal condemns the cardinals of Dante's time.

context: Cephas, "rock" in Aramaic, is the name Jesus gave Simon Peter (John 1:42). He stands here for the poverty of the first leaders of the Church.
In Acts 9:15 God calls Paul his "chosen vessel". Inferno 2 uses the same name for him.

note: Jesus told the disciples he sent out to eat whatever was set before them in the houses that took them in (Luke 10). The apostles lived on what they were given.

The bishops and cardinals of Dante's day, shepherds of the Christian flock. They are so fat that they need a servant on each side to prop them up, one to lead the horse and one to carry the train of the robe.

quote: two beasts go beneath one skin
note: The prelate's fur-lined cloak is so wide that it covers his horse as well. Two animals under one hide: the horse and its rider. It is one of the sharpest jokes in Paradiso.
God's patience, which puts up with all this and has not yet struck.

quote: a cry of such loud sound
note: The silence of Saturn breaks. The souls shout together in anger at what Peter Damian has described, so loudly that Dante can't make out the words. Beatrice explains in Canto 22 that it was a prayer for God's vengeance on the corrupt clergy.
